EXPTIME: exposure-time Poisson model

Source: vignettes/exptime.Rmd
exptime.Rmd
library(bssd)

Model

Schnell and Ball (2016) monitor the rate of an adverse event of special interest with blinded data: for each enrolled subject, the follow-up time \(t_i\) and the number of events \(y_i\). With the unknown treatment assignment \(a_i\) (1 for study drug), \[ Y_i \mid a_i \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_{a_i} t_i), \quad a_i \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(k / (k + 1)), \quad \lambda_c \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha_c, \beta_c), \quad \lambda_d \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha_d, \beta_d), \] where \(k\) is the randomization ratio of study drug to control. The prior of the control rate is informative (from historical control data), and the prior of the study drug rate is weaker. A safety signal is raised when the posterior probability that \(\lambda_d\) exceeds a critical rate is larger than a threshold.

Summing over the assignment of each subject gives the likelihood \[ \prod_i \left[ \frac{1}{k + 1} \lambda_c^{y_i} e^{-\lambda_c t_i} + \frac{k}{k + 1} \lambda_d^{y_i} e^{-\lambda_d t_i} \right], \] so the posterior is two-dimensional. Schnell and Ball (2016) sample it by Gibbs sampling; exptime_post() integrates it numerically. With event indicators as y and the times at risk (up to the first event) as t, the model is the exponential model for the time to the first event, which is how sim_oc() uses it (model "EXPTIME").

Example

The priors of the case study of Schnell and Ball (2016): 339 events in 26,064 person-months of historical control data, and for the study drug the same data discounted to one hundredth plus 4 events in 167 person-months from a phase 2 study. The critical rate is 20% above the control rate 0.013, and the threshold is 0.62.

set.seed(1)
n <- 600
t <- runif(n, 2, 18)
drug <- rbinom(n, 1, 2 / 3)
y <- rpois(n, ifelse(drug == 1, 0.016, 0.011) * t)
c(subjects = n, events = sum(y), person_months = round(sum(t)))
#>      subjects        events person_months 
#>           600            92          6019
fit <- exptime_post(y, t, k = 2, prior_c = c(339, 26064),
                    prior_d = c(339 / 100 + 4, 26064 / 100 + 167),
                    rate0 = 1.2 * 0.013, cutoff = 0.62)
fit
#> Model: EXPTIME 
#> Tested quantity: event rate lambda_d of study drug
#> P(lambda_d > 0.0156 | data) = 0.6252
#> Signal (posterior probability > 0.62): yes
#> Posterior of r: mean 1.262, median 1.253, 95% interval (0.9105, 1.667)
#> Posterior of lambda_d: mean 0.01638, median 0.0163, 95% interval (0.01223, 0.02097)

The posterior probability of the rate ratio is also returned:

fit$probs
#>      drug     ratio 
#> 0.6251912 0.9207968

Priors can be elicited from two quantiles with elicit_prior(); for example, 50% sure that a rate is below 0.5 and 75% sure that it is below 2:

elicit_prior(c(0.5, 2), c(0.5, 0.75), "gamma")
#>     shape      rate 
#> 0.3460050 0.2089832

Numerical integration

The posterior is integrated over \(\log \lambda_c\) by Gauss-Legendre quadrature. For each of its nodes, the interval of \(\lambda_d\) that holds the conditional posterior mass is located on the scale \(z = \Phi^{-1}(F_d(\lambda_d))\), where \(F_d\) is the prior distribution function of \(\lambda_d\), and the density is interpolated at Chebyshev points in \(z\) or in \(F_d(\lambda_d)\), whichever represents it more accurately. The first scale keeps the far tails of an informative prior, which matters when the data put \(\lambda_d\) many prior standard deviations above its prior mean; the second keeps a vague prior from creating long tails. The posterior probability of a threshold that depends on \(\lambda_c\) (such as the rate ratio) is obtained from the Chebyshev series of each row. Compared with independent Python computations on dense grids split exactly at the thresholds (inst/validation/validate_methods_python.R, three data sets including one with a study drug rate far in the upper tail of the prior of Schnell and Ball, 2016), the largest absolute difference of the 5 posterior probabilities is 2.9e-09, and all 32 compared quantities are PASS.

Comparison with MCMC

A JAGS model with the latent treatment assignments (inst/validation/validate_jags_methods.R, 4 chains of 50,000 draws) gives the following results for a data set of 60 subjects.

quantity MCMC bssd judgement
P(lambda_d > 0.03 | data) 0.3926 0.3912 PASS
P(r > 1.2 | data) 0.6383 0.6385 PASS
posterior mean of lambda_c 0.0204 0.0204 PASS
MCMC proportion below the bssd posterior median 0.5000 0.5001 PASS

Reproduction of Schnell and Ball (2016)

inst/reproduce/reproduce_Schnell2016.R generates the simulated case study with the data generation of the authors’ code and seed 1, and compares Table 2 and the prior elicitation example: 27 PASS, 3 EXPLAINED, 1 FAIL and 16 INFO. The posterior summaries in Table 2 are Monte Carlo estimates of the authors’ Gibbs sampler, whose Metropolis step uses Poisson probabilities of the arm totals; bssd computes the posterior of the subject-level model above. The reasons for the items that are not PASS are in inst/reproduce/results/SUMMARY.md.

The authors’ code was run outside the package (the code has no stated license): with seed 1 it reproduces the published probabilities, and with 200,000 draws its sampler and a sampler with the subject-level likelihood give the following probabilities that the study drug rate exceeds 0.0156.

month published authors_code authors_sampler subject_level_sampler bssd
4 0.710 0.710 0.679 0.720 0.721
8 0.518 0.518 0.498 0.601 0.603
12 0.872 0.872 0.839 0.931 0.932
16 0.968 0.968 0.973 0.996 0.996

The simulation of Table 1 (inst/reproduce/reproduce_Schnell2016_simulation.R) has not been run for this installation.

References

Schnell, P. M. and Ball, G. (2016). A Bayesian exposure-time method for clinical trial safety monitoring with blinded data. Therapeutic Innovation & Regulatory Science, 50(6), 833–838. https://doi.org/10.1177/2168479016656702
